svg.text: Figure 2 redrawn — the identity path in green, the residual branch in blue

g.data-tip: The input is carried around the weight layers unchanged and added back. It holds no matrix, so it adds no parameter and no convolution: the paper says identity shortcut connections add neither extra parameter nor computational complexity.
g.text: identity shortcut — x carried through unchanged, parameter-free

g.data-tip: The input to this group of layers. It is used twice: once as the input to the weight layers and once, unmodified, on the shortcut.

a.data-tip: A convolution, with batch normalisation right after it. In the paper's notation this contributes the W1 in F = W2 sigma(W1 x); biases are omitted to simplify the notation.

g.data-tip: The sigma in F = W2 sigma(W1 x). This nonlinearity sits inside the residual branch, between the two weight layers.

a.data-tip: The W2 of the residual branch. Its output is what gets added to x, so it must have the same shape as x for the addition to be defined.

g.data-tip: Not a concatenation and not a gate. The two feature maps are added channel by channel, position by position, with no learned weight anywhere in the operation.
The paper adopts the second nonlinearity after the addition. That ordering is the one the same authors revisited a few months later in Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks.
The block computes H(x) = F(x) + x and passes it through the outer ReLU. The layers were asked to fit F, the residual, rather than H, the full mapping.

svg.text: F(x) — the residual function; every parameter of the block is in here

a.data-tip: The block is defined in Section 3.2 of the paper as y = F(x, {Wi}) + x, where F is the residual mapping to be learned.
a.text: x — the block input, and the thing the shortcut carries
weight layer — a convolution with batch normalisation after it
F(x) — what the two weight layers compute, biases omitted
+ — element-wise addition of two feature maps, channel by channel
the second ReLU is applied after the addition, not before it

a.data-tip: Because the shortcut costs nothing, a plain net and a residual net can be built with identical depth, width, parameter count and FLOPs. Without that, the comparison in Table 2 would be confounded.
a.text: What the shortcut costs, and why that matters
Parameters added: none — there is no matrix on the identity path.
Computation added: one element-wise add per activation, which the
paper calls negligible next to the convolutions.
So plain and residual nets can be matched on depth, width, parameter
count and FLOPs — which is what makes the Table 2 comparison fair.
